165-
166--- ## Inductively Defined Propositions
167-
168--- In the Logic chapter, we looked at several ways of writing
169--- propositions, including conjunction, disjunction, and
170--- existential quantification.
171-
172--- In this chapter, we bring yet another new tool into the mix:
173--- *inductively defined propositions*.
174-
175--- To begin, some examples...
176-
177--- ### Example: The Collatz Conjecture
178-
179--- The *Collatz Conjecture* is a famous open problem in number
180--- theory.
181-
182--- Its statement is quite simple. First, we define a function
183--- `csf` on numbers, as follows (where `csf` stands for
184--- "Collatz step function"):
185-
186-def div2 (n : Nat) : Nat :=
187-  match n with
188-  | 0      => 0
189-  | 1      => 0
190-  | n' + 2 => div2 n' + 1
191-
192-def csf (n : Nat) : Nat :=
193-  if n.even then div2 n
194-  else (3 * n) + 1
195-
196--- Next, we look at what happens when we repeatedly apply `csf`
197--- to some given starting number. For example, `csf 12` is `6`,
198--- and `csf 6` is `3`, so by repeatedly applying `csf` we get
199--- the sequence `12, 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1`.
200-
201--- Similarly, if we start with `19`, we get the longer sequence
202--- `19,
203--- 58, 29, 88, 44, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8,
204--- 4, 2, 1`.
205-
206--- Both of these sequences eventually reach `1`. The question
207--- posed by Collatz was: Is the sequence starting from *any*
208--- positive natural number guaranteed to reach `1` eventually?
209-
210--- To formalize this question in Lean, we might try to define a
211--- recursive *function* that calculates the total number of
212--- steps that it takes for such a sequence to reach `1`. You
213--- can write this definition in a standard programming
214--- language, but it is rejected by Lean's termination checker,
215--- since the argument to the recursive call, `csf n`, is not
216--- "obviously smaller" than `n`.
217-
218-sf_expect_failure
219-  def reaches1In (n : Nat) : Nat :=
220-    if n == 1 then 0
221-    else 1 + reaches1In (csf n)
222-
223--- fail to show termination for
224---   reaches1In
225--- with errors
226--- failed to infer structural recursion:
227--- Cannot use parameter n:
228---   failed to eliminate recursive application
229---     reaches1In (csf n)
230-
231-
232--- failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
233---   - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
234---   - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
235---   - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
236--- n : Nat
237--- h✝ : ¬(n == 1) = true
238--- ⊢ csf n < n
239-
240--- Indeed, this isn't just a pointless limitation: functions in
241--- Lean are required to be total, to ensure logical
242--- consistency.
243-
244--- Moreover, we can't fix it by devising a more clever
245--- termination checker: deciding whether this particular
246--- function is total would be equivalent to settling the
247--- Collatz conjecture!
248-
249--- Another idea could be to express the concept "eventually
250--- reaches `1` in the Collatz sequence" as a *recursively
251--- defined property* of numbers `CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop`.
252--- This is also rejected by the termination checker. In
253--- principle, we could convince Lean that `div2 n` is smaller
254--- than `n` by supplying an appropriate proof. However, we
255--- still can't convince it that `(3 * n) + 1` is smaller than
256--- `n`!
257-
258-sf_expect_failure
259-  def CollatzHoldsFor (n : Nat) : Prop :=
260-    match n with
261-    | 0 => False
262-    | 1 => True
263-    | _ => if n.even then CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
264-                     else CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)
265-
266--- fail to show termination for
267---   CollatzHoldsFor
268--- with errors
269--- failed to infer structural recursion:
270--- Cannot use parameter n:
271---   failed to eliminate recursive application
272---     CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
273-
274-
275--- failed to prove termination, possible solutions:
276---   - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
277---   - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
278---   - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
279--- n x✝ : Nat
280--- h✝ : n.even = true
281--- ⊢ div2 n < x✝
282-
283--- Fortunately, there is another way to do it: We can express
284--- the concept "reaches `1` eventually in the Collatz sequence"
285--- as an *inductively defined property* of numbers.
286--- Intuitively, this property is defined by a set of rules:
287-
288---                 ─────────────────── (chf_one)
289---                  CollatzHoldsFor 1
290-
291---   even n = true     CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
292---   ─────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_even)
293---                  CollatzHoldsFor n
294-
295---   even n = false    CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)
296---   ─────────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_odd)
297---                  CollatzHoldsFor n
298-
299--- So there are three ways to prove that a number `n`
300--- eventually reaches `1` in the Collatz sequence:
301-
302--- - `n` is `1`;
303--- - `n` is even and `div2 n` eventually reaches `1`;
304--- - `n` is odd and `(3 * n) + 1` eventually reaches `1`.
305-
306--- We can prove that a number reaches `1` by constructing a
307--- (finite) derivation using these rules. For instance, here is
308--- the derivation proving that `12` reaches `1` (where we leave
309--- out the evenness/oddness premises):
310-
311---   ─────────────────────── (chf_one)
312---     CollatzHoldsFor 1
313---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
314---     CollatzHoldsFor 2
315---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
316---     CollatzHoldsFor 4
317---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
318---     CollatzHoldsFor 8
319---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
320---     CollatzHoldsFor 16
321---   ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
322---     CollatzHoldsFor 5
323---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
324---     CollatzHoldsFor 10
325---   ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
326---     CollatzHoldsFor 3
327---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
328---     CollatzHoldsFor 6
329---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
330---     CollatzHoldsFor 12
331-
332--- Formally in Lean, the `CollatzHoldsFor` property is
333--- *inductively defined*:
334-
335-inductive CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop where
336-  | chf_one  : CollatzHoldsFor 1
337-  | chf_even {n : Nat} (h₁ : n.even = true)
338-    (h₂ : CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)) : CollatzHoldsFor n
339-  | chf_odd  {n : Nat} (h₁ : n.even = false)
340-    (h₂ : CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)) : CollatzHoldsFor n
341-
342--- For particular numbers, we can now prove that the Collatz
343--- sequence reaches `1` (we'll look more closely at how it
344--- works a bit later in the chapter). Each step applies a rule
345--- and discharges the boolean evenness premise by `rfl`; the
346--- recursive premise is then reduced by the kernel from
347--- `CollatzHoldsFor (div2 12)` to `CollatzHoldsFor 6`, etc.
348-
349-example : CollatzHoldsFor 12 := by
350-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
351-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
352-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd;   rfl
353-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
354-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd;   rfl
355-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
356-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
357-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
358-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
359-  exact CollatzHoldsFor.chf_one
360-
361--- The Collatz conjecture then states that the sequence
362--- beginning from *any* positive number reaches `1`:
363-
364-def Collatz := ∀ n, n ≠ 0 → CollatzHoldsFor n
365-
366--- If you succeed in proving this conjecture, you've got a
367--- bright future as a number theorist! But don't spend too long
368--- on it ─ it's been open since 1937.
369-
370--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
371---     We may want to add an exercise later proving false if
372---     one assumes Collatz' conjecture without the `n ≠ 0`
373---     assumption. We had that mistake in the script for years
374---     and no one noticed, wow!
375---
376---     `theorem Collatz0' {n} (h₀ : n = 0) : ¬ CollatzHoldsFor n := by
377---       intro h; induction h
378---       case chf_one => contradiction
379---       case chf_even ih => apply ih; rw [h₀]; dsimp [div2]
380---       case chf_odd h _ _ => rw [h₀] at h; dsimp [Nat.even] at h; contradiction
381---
382---     theorem Collatz0 : ¬ (∀ n, CollatzHoldsFor n) := by
383---       intro h; apply Collatz0'; rfl; apply h`
384-
385--- ### Example: Binary Relation for Comparing Numbers
386-
387--- A binary *relation* on a set `α` has Lean type
388--- `α → α → Prop`. This is a family of propositions
389--- parameterized by two elements of `α` ─ i.e., a proposition
390--- about pairs of elements of `α`.
391-
392--- For example, one familiar binary relation on `Nat` is
393--- `Le : Nat → Nat → Prop`, the less-than-or-equal-to relation,
394--- which can be inductively defined by the following two rules:
395-
396---     ─────── (le_refl)
397---     Le n n
398-
399---     Le n m
400---   ──────────── (le_step)
401---   Le n (m + 1)
402-
403-namespace LePlayground
404-
405-inductive Le : Nat → Nat → Prop where
406-  | refl {n : Nat}                : Le n n
407-  | step {n m : Nat} (h : Le n m) : Le n (m + 1)
408-
409-scoped infix:50 (priority := high) " ≤ " => Le
410-
411-example : 3 ≤ 5 := by
412-  apply Le.step; apply Le.step; exact Le.refl
413-
414-end LePlayground
415-
416--- ### Example: Transitive Closure
417-
418--- Another example: The *transitive closure* of a relation `R`
419--- is the smallest relation that contains `R` and that is
420--- transitive. This can be defined by the following two rules:
421-
422---                 R x y
423---            ─────────────── (t_step)
424---            ClosTrans R x y
425-
426---   ClosTrans R x y    ClosTrans R y z
427---   ──────────────────────────────────── (t_trans)
428---            ClosTrans R x z
429-
430--- In Lean this looks as follows:
431-
432-inductive ClosTrans {α : Type} (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
433-  | t_step {x y : α} (h : R x y) : ClosTrans R x y
434-  | t_trans {x y z : α}
435-    (h₁ : ClosTrans R x y)
436-    (h₂ : ClosTrans R y z) :
437-    ClosTrans R x z
438-
439--- For example, suppose we define a "parent of" relation on a
440--- group of people...
441-
442-inductive Person : Type where
443-  | sage
444-  | cleo
445-  | ridley
446-  | moss
447-
448-inductive ParentOf : Person → Person → Prop where
449-  | po_SC : ParentOf .sage .cleo
450-  | po_SR : ParentOf .sage .ridley
451-  | po_CM : ParentOf .cleo .moss
452-
453--- The `ParentOf` relation is not transitive, but we can define
454--- an "ancestor of" relation as its transitive closure:
455-
456-def AncestorOf : Person → Person → Prop := ClosTrans ParentOf
457-
458--- Here is a derivation showing that `sage` is an ancestor of
459--- `moss`:
460-
461---    ——————————————————— (po_SC)     ——————————————————— (po_CM)
462---    ParentOf .sage .cleo            ParentOf .cleo .moss
463---   ————————————————————— (t_step)  ————————————————————— (t_step)
464---   AncestorOf .sage .cleo          AncestorOf .cleo .moss
465---   ———————————————————————————————————————————————————— (t_trans)
466---                   AncestorOf .sage .moss
467-
468-example : AncestorOf .sage .moss := by
469-  apply ClosTrans.t_trans
470-  . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_SC
471-  . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_CM
472-
473--- Note to developers:
474---     HIDE: CH: A simple exercise could be nice here?
475-
476--- ### Example: Reflexive and Transitive Closure
477-
478--- As another example, the *reflexive and transitive closure*
479--- of a relation `R` is the smallest relation that contains `R`
480--- and that is reflexive and transitive. This can be defined by
481--- the following three rules (where we added a reflexivity rule
482--- to `ClosTrans`):
483-
484---                      R x y
485---            ——————————————————————— (rt_step)
486---              ClosReflTrans R x y
487-
488---            ——————————————————————— (rt_refl)
489---              ClosReflTrans R x x
490-
491---      ClosReflTrans R x y    ClosReflTrans R y z
492---   —————————————————————————————————————————————— (rt_trans)
493---              ClosReflTrans R x z
494-
495-inductive ClosReflTrans {α : Type} (R : α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
496-  | rt_step {x y : α} (h : R x y) : ClosReflTrans R x y
497-  | rt_refl {x : α} : ClosReflTrans R x x
498-  | rt_trans {x y z : α}
499-    (h₁ : ClosReflTrans R x y)
500-    (h₂ : ClosReflTrans R y z) :
501-    ClosReflTrans R x z
502-
503--- For instance, this enables an equivalent definition of the
504--- Collatz conjecture. First we define a binary relation
505--- corresponding to the "Collatz step function" `csf`:
506-
507-def CS (n m : Nat) : Prop := csf n = m
508-
509--- This Collatz step relation can be used in conjunction with
510--- the reflexive and transitive closure operation to define a
511--- *Collatz multi-step* (`CMS`) relation, expressing that a
512--- number `n` reaches another number `m` in zero or more
513--- Collatz steps:
514-
515-def CMS (n m : Nat) : Prop := ClosReflTrans CS n m
516-def Collatz' : Prop := ∀ (n : Nat), n ≠ 0 → CMS n 1
517-
518--- Note to developers:
519---     HIDE: CH: Would it be helpful to add an exercise later
520---     proving CMS equivalent to CollatzHoldsFor?
521-
522--- ### Example: Permutations
523-
524--- The familiar mathematical concept of *permutation* also has
525--- an elegant formulation as an inductive relation. For
526--- simplicity, let's focus on permutations of lists with
527--- exactly three elements.
528-
529--- We can define such permutations by the following rules:
530-
531---      ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap12)
532---      Perm3 [a, b, c] [b, a, c]
533-
534---      ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap23)
535---      Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, c, b]
536-
537---   Perm3 l₁ l₂       Perm3 l₂ l₃
538---   ───────────────────────────── (perm3_trans)
539---            Perm3 l₁ l₃
540-
541--- For instance we can derive `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]` as
542--- follows:
543-
544---   ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap12)   ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap23)
545---   Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 1, 3]                  Perm3 [2, 1, 3] [2, 3, 1]
546---   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── (perm3_trans)   ───────────────────────── (perm3_swap12)
547---   Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 3, 1]                                                            Perm3 [2, 3, 1] [3, 2, 1]
548---   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── (perm3_trans)
549---   Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]
550-
551--- In Lean, we can define `Perm3` as follows:
552-
553-inductive Perm3 {α : Type} : List α → List α → Prop where
554-  | perm3_swap12 {x y z : α} : Perm3 [x, y, z] [y, x, z]
555-  | perm3_swap23 {x y z : α} : Perm3 [x, y, z] [x, z, y]
556-  | perm3_trans {l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α}
557-    (h₁₂ : Perm3 l₁ l₂)
558-    (h₂₃ : Perm3 l₂ l₃) :
559-    Perm3 l₁ l₃
560-
561--- ### Example: Evenness (yet again)
562-
563--- We've already seen two ways of stating a proposition that a
564--- number `n` is even: We can say
565-
566--- (1) `Nat.even n = true` (using the recursive boolean
567--- function `Nat.even`), or
568-
569--- (2) `∃ k, n = Nat.double k` (using an existential
570--- quantifier).
571-
572--- A third possibility, which we'll use as a simple running
573--- example in this chapter, is to say that a number is even if
574--- we can *establish* its evenness from the following two
575--- rules:
576-
577---       ———— (ev_0)
578---       Ev 0
579-
580---       Ev n
581---   —————————————— (ev_succ_succ)
582---     Ev (n + 2)
583-
584--- To illustrate how this new definition of evenness works,
585--- let's imagine using it to show that `4` is even:
586-
587---                 ———— (ev_0)
588---                 Ev 0
589---          ———————————————————— (ev_succ_succ)
590---          Ev (.succ (.succ 0))
591---   ——————————————————————————————————— (ev_succ_succ)
592---   Ev (.succ (.succ (.succ (.succ 0))))
593-
594--- We can translate the informal definition of evenness from
595--- above into a formal `inductive` declaration, where each "way
596--- that a number can be even" corresponds to a separate
597--- constructor:
598-
599-inductive Ev : Nat → Prop where
600-  | ev_0                              : Ev 0
601-  | ev_succ_succ {n : Nat} (h : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
602-
603--- There are both similarities and a few differences between
604--- inductive *properties* like `Ev` and the inductive *types*
605--- like `Nat` or `List` that we have been using throughout the
606--- course:
607-
608-sf_expect_failure
609-  inductive List (α : Type) : Type where
610-    | nil                       : List α
611-    | cons (x : α) (l : List α) : List α
612-
613--- The most important difference is that the constructors of
614--- `Ev`, `Ev.ev_0` and `Ev.ev_succ_succ`, yield different types
615--- (`Ev 0` and `Ev (n + 2)`), whereas the `List` constructors
616--- both build `List α` values.
617-
618--- We can think of the inductive definition of `Ev` as defining
619--- a Lean property `Ev : Nat → Prop`, together with two
620--- "evidence constructors":
621-
622-#check Ev.ev_0         -- Ev 0
623-#check Ev.ev_succ_succ -- ∀ (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
624-
625--- These evidence constructors can be thought of as "primitive
626--- evidence of evenness", and they can be used later on just
627--- like proven theorems. In particular, we can use Lean's
628--- `apply` and `exact` tactics with the constructor names to
629--- obtain evidence for `Ev` of particular numbers...
630-
631-namespace Ev
632-
633-example : Ev 4 := by
634-  apply ev_succ_succ; apply ev_succ_succ; exact ev_0
635-
636--- ... or we can use function application syntax to combine
637--- several constructors:
638-
639-example : Ev 4 := by
640-  exact ev_succ_succ (ev_succ_succ ev_0)
641-
642--- ... or we can also use the `constructor` tactic we saw
643--- earlier to select the appropriate inductive constructor:
644-
645-example : Ev 4 := by
646-  constructor; constructor; constructor
647-
648--- In this way, we can also prove theorems that have hypotheses
649--- involving `Ev`.
650-
651-theorem plus4 (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Ev (4 + n) := by
652-  rw [Nat.add_comm]
653-  exact (ev_succ_succ (ev_succ_succ h))
654-
655-end Ev
656-
657--- ### Constructing Evidence for Permutations
658-
659--- Similarly we can apply the evidence constructors to obtain
660--- evidence of `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]`:
661-
662-namespace Perm3
663-
664-theorem rev : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
665-  apply perm3_trans (l₂:= [2, 3, 1])
666-  . apply perm3_trans (l₂ := [2, 1, 3])
667-    . apply perm3_swap12
668-    . apply perm3_swap23
669-  . apply perm3_swap12
670-
671--- And again we can equivalently use function application
672--- syntax to combine several constructors. (Note that the Lean
673--- type checker can infer not only types, but also `Nat`s and
674--- `List`s, when they are clear from the context.)
675-
676-theorem rev' : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
677-  exact (perm3_trans
678-          (perm3_trans perm3_swap12 perm3_swap23)
679-          perm3_swap12)
680-
681--- So the informal derivation trees we drew above are not too
682--- far from what's happening formally. Formally we're using the
683--- evidence constructors to build *evidence trees*, similar to
684--- the finite trees we built using the constructors of data
685--- types such as `Nat`, `List`, binary trees, etc.
686-
687-end Perm3
688-
689--- ## Using Evidence in Proofs
690-
691--- Besides *constructing* evidence that numbers are even, we
692--- can also *destruct* such evidence, reasoning about how it
693--- could have been built.
694-
695--- Defining `Ev` with an `inductive` declaration tells Lean not
696--- only that the constructors `Ev.ev_0` and `Ev.ev_succ_succ`
697--- are valid ways to build evidence that some number is `Ev`,
698--- but also that these two constructors are the *only* ways to
699--- build evidence that numbers are `Ev`.
700-
701--- In other words, if someone gives us evidence `e` for the
702--- proposition `Ev n`, then we know that `e` must be one of two
703--- things:
704-
705--- - `e = ev_0` and `n = 0`, or
706-
707--- - `e = ev_succ_succ n' e'` and `n = n' + 2`, where `e'` is
708---   evidence for `Ev n'`.
709-
710--- This suggests that it should be possible to do *case
711--- analysis* and even *induction* on evidence of evenness...
712-
713--- ### Destructing and Inverting Evidence
714-
715--- We can prove our characterization of evidence for `Ev n`,
716--- using `cases`.
717-
718-theorem ev_inversion (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) :
719-    (n = 0) ∨ ∃ n', n = n' + 2 ∧ Ev n' := by
720-  cases h with
721-  | ev_0 => left; rfl
722-  | @ev_succ_succ n h => right; exists n
723-
724--- Facts like this are often called "inversion lemmas" because
725--- they allow us to "invert" some given information to reason
726--- about all the different ways it could have been derived.
727-
728--- _Quiz:_
729-
730--- Which tactics are needed to prove this goal?
731-
732---   ∀ (n : Nat), Ev n → n = 1 → true = false
733-
734--- (A) `cases` (B) `contradiction` (C) Both `cases` and
735--- `contradiction` (D) these tactics are not sufficient to
736--- solve the goal.
737-
738--- We can use the inversion lemma that we proved above to help
739--- structure proofs:
740-
741-theorem ev_succ_succ_ev (n : Nat) (h : Ev (n + 2)) : Ev n := by
742-  apply ev_inversion at h
743-  obtain ⟨⟨⟩⟩ | ⟨n', ⟨h₁,  h₂⟩⟩ := h
744-  injections h₁ heq
745-  subst heq
746-  exact h₂
747-
748--- We've provided a handy tactic called `inversion` that does
749--- the work of our inversion lemma and more besides.
750-
751-theorem ev_succ_succ_ev' (n : Nat) (h : Ev (n + 2)) : Ev n := by
752-  inversion h; assumption
753-
754--- We can use `inversion` to re-prove some theorems from
755--- Tactics.
756-
757--- Note that `inversion` also works on equality propositions.
758-
759-theorem inversion_ex1 (n m o : Nat) (h : [n, m] = [o, o]) : [n] = [m] := by
760-  inversion h; rfl
761-
762-theorem inversion_ex2 n (h : n + 1 = 0) : 2 + 2 = 5 := by
763-  inversion h
764-
765--- The `inversion` tactic works on any `h : p` where `p` is
766--- defined inductively:
767-
768--- - For each constructor of `p`, make a subgoal where `h` is
769---   constrained by the form of this constructor.
770-
771--- - Discard contradictory subgoals (such as `ev_0` above).
772-
773--- - Generate auxiliary equalities (as with `ev_succ_succ`
774---   above).
775-

777---     The wording there is totally awkward!
778-
779--- _Quiz:_
780-
781--- Note to developers:
782---     LY: Not quite a fair question because this is the first
783---     time they are facing a situation where the index does
784---     not start with a constructor.
785-
786--- Which tactics are needed to prove this goal, in addition to
787--- `apply` or `exact`?
788-
789---   ∀ n, Ev (2 + n) → Ev n
790-
791--- (A) `inversion` (B) `inversion`, `injections` (C)
792--- `inversion`, `rw [Nat.add_comm]` (D) `inversion`,
793--- `rw [Nat.add_comm]`, `injections`

796--- our earlier notion (the one based on `Nat.double`).

804-        since `Ev` is mentioned in a premise, this strategy seems

856--- ### Induction on Evidence
857-
858--- If this story feels familiar, it is no coincidence: We
859--- encountered similar problems in the Induction chapter, when
860--- trying to use case analysis to prove results that required
861--- induction. And once again the solution is... induction!
862-
863--- Let's try proving that lemma again:
864-
865-theorem Nat.ev_Even (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Even n := by
866-  induction h with
867-  -- h = ev_0
868-  | ev_0 => exists 0 -- (`0 = double 0` is closed by `exists`'s final `rfl`)
869-  -- h = ev_succ_succ n' h', with ih : Even n'
870-  | ev_succ_succ h' ih =>
871-    let ⟨k, hk⟩ := ih
872-    exists k + 1; rw [double_succ, hk]

103-

226--- ### Tip: the `rw` tactic
227-
228--- As you've probably noticed, a common pattern in Lean proofs
229--- is `rewrite [...]` followed by `rfl`. There is a tactic that
230--- combines these two steps: `rw [...]` will automatically
231--- close the goal if the rewrite makes the goal true by
232--- definition. For example, instead of writing
233-
234---   rewrite [double_zero]; rfl
235-
236--- We could write this:
237-
238---   rw [double_zero]
239-
240--- If `rw` leaves a goal that looks definitionally true, try
241--- adding `rfl` after it.

327--- ### Aside: Using Code Actions to Generate Match Skeletons
328-
329--- Lean's language server can suggest *code actions*, which are
330--- small editor commands that modify the source code.
331-
332--- In VS Code, a lightbulb icon appears on the left when a code
333--- action is available at your cursor.
334-
335--- Let's look at an example code action using `induction`. For
336--- example, suppose we start with the following incomplete
337--- proof:
338-
339-sf_expect_failure
340-  example (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
341-    induction n
342-
343--- Put your cursor on `induction n` and open the code action
344--- menu. You should see "Generate an explicit pattern match for
345--- 'induction'." in the list. If you choose this action, Lean
346--- adds an explicit branch for each constructor:
347-
348-example (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
349-  induction n with
350-  | zero => sorry
351-  | succ n ih => sorry
352-
353--- This gives us basic structure of the proof without requiring
354--- us to write each branch by hand. We can then focus on
355--- proving each case.
356-
357--- One possible proof is:
358-
359-example (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
360-  induction n with
361-  | zero => exact (beq_self zero)
362-  | succ n ih => rw [Nat.beq, ih]
363-
364--- The same trick also works for `match` expressions. For
365--- example, suppose we start with
366-
367-sf_expect_failure
368-  def isZero (n : Nat) : Bool :=
369-    match n
370-
371--- Lean can generate the missing branches:
372-
373-sf_expect_failure
374-  def isZero (n : Nat) : Bool :=
375-    match n with
376-    | .zero => _
377-    | .succ n => _
378-
379--- Now you just have to replace the holes `_` with your
380--- definition. You can use code actions freely to fill out
381--- `induction`, `case`, and `match` branches while working with
382--- this book.
383-
384--- By default, `rewrite` and `rw` rewrite left to right, i.e.,
385--- they transform the goal (or a hypothesis) from the form on
386--- the left side of the equality to the right side. To rewrite
387--- from right to left, use `rewrite [← h]` or `rw [← h]`, where
388--- `←` is entered as `\l` or `\<-`.
389-
390--- These exercises state facts that will be used later. We
391--- don't need to work them in class.

446--- ### A New Tactic Combinator
447-
448--- New tactic combinator: `t₁ <;> t₂` runs `t₁`, then runs `t₂`
449--- on every subgoal produced by `t₁`.
450-
451-example (b : Bool) : (b || true) = true := by
452-  cases b <;> rfl
453-
454--- This is short for:
455-
456-example (b : Bool) : (b || true) = true := by
457-  cases b with
458-  | false => rfl
459-  | true  => rfl
460-
461--- We can also chain `<;>`s.
462-
463-example (b c : Bool) : (b && c) = (c && b) := by
464-  cases b <;> cases c <;> rfl

549-
550--- The opposite direction — starting with a `Bin`, converting
551--- to `Nat`, then converting back to `Bin` — turns out to be
552--- problematic. That is, the following "theorem" does not hold.

558--- modified version of it. We'll start with some lemmas that
559--- might seem unrelated but will turn out to be relevant.

1-import LF.Induction

4-import SFLCompat
5-
6--- # Lists: Working with Structured Data
7-
8-namespace Lists
9-
10--- ## Pairs of Numbers
11-
12--- An inductive definition of pairs of numbers. It has just one
13--- constructor, taking two arguments:
14-
15-inductive NatProd where
16-  | pair (n1 n2 : Nat)
17-
18-#check (NatProd.pair 3 5)
19-
20--- Note to developers (Mike Hicks @mwhicks1):
21---     I would have expected us to have `namespace NatProd`
22---     here when defining the following functions, so we don't
23---     need qualifiers. We've already full explained namespaces
24---     back in Basics. Some of the text below mentions using
25---     the `NatProd` prefix specifically, but I think you can
26---     drop it and it will stick work.
27-
28--- Functions for extracting the first and second components of
29--- a pair can then be defined by pattern matching.
30-
31-def NatProd.fst (p : NatProd) : Nat :=
32-  match p with
33-  | .pair x _ => x
34-
35-def NatProd.snd (p : NatProd) : Nat :=
36-  match p with
37-  | .pair _ y => y
38-
39--- Defining these functions with the `NatProd` type name
40--- qualifying their name allows us to use them with `.`
41--- notation:
42-
43-example : (NatProd.pair 3 5).fst = 3 := by rfl
44-
45--- A nicer notation for pairs:
46-
47-example : (⟨3, 5⟩ : NatProd).fst = 3 := by rfl
48-
49--- The anonymous constructor can be used in both expressions
50--- and in pattern matches.
51-
52-def NatProd.fst' (p : NatProd) : Nat :=
53-  match p with
54-  | ⟨x, _⟩ => x
55-
56-def NatProd.snd' (p : NatProd) : Nat :=
57-  match p with
58-  | ⟨_, y⟩ => y
59-
60-def NatProd.swap (p : NatProd) : NatProd :=
61-  ⟨snd p, fst p⟩
62-
63--- To expose the structure of a pair, use `cases` (or
64--- destructuring).
65-
66-theorem surjective_pairing : ∀ p : NatProd,
67-    p = ⟨p.fst, p.snd⟩ := by
68-  intro ⟨n, m⟩; rfl
69-
70-theorem surjective_pairing_cases (p : NatProd) :
71-    p = ⟨p.fst, p.snd⟩ := by
72-  cases p; rfl
73-
74--- ## Structures
75-
76--- Lean's `structure` is shorthand for a single-constructor
77--- `inductive` with the accessors auto-generated.
78-
79-structure NatProd' where
80-  fst : Nat
81-  snd : Nat
82-
83-#check (NatProd'.mk 3 5)
84-example : (NatProd'.mk 3 5).fst = 3 := by rfl
85-example : (⟨3, 5⟩ : NatProd').fst = 3 := by rfl

87--- ## Lists of Numbers
88-
89--- An inductive definition of *lists* of numbers:
90-
91-inductive NatList : Type where
92-  | nil
93-  | cons (n : Nat) (l : NatList)
94-
95--- By convention, we place the operations (functions) of an
96--- inductive type inside the namespace implicitly created by
97--- that type's definition.
98-
99-namespace NatList
100-
101--- Some notation for lists to make our lives easier:
102-
103--- Don't worry too much about how this works.
104-
105--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: List syntax
106-
107--- We first define `::` as right-associative notation for
108--- `cons`, and then define list notation as a *macro*, allowing
109--- us to write `[1, 2]` instead of `1 :: 2 :: []`. The
110--- *unexpander* reverses the macro, translating list syntax
111--- back to cons syntax.
112-
113-scoped infixr:65 (priority := high) " :: " => cons
114-scoped macro (priority := high) "[" elems:term,* "]" : term => do
115-  elems.getElems.foldrM (``(cons $(⟨·⟩) $(⟨·⟩))) (← ``(nil))
116-
117-@[scoped app_unexpander nil]
118-def unexpandNil : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
119-  | `($_) => `([])
120-
121-@[scoped app_unexpander cons]
122-def unexpandCons : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
123-  | `($_ $x []) => `([$x])
124-  | `($_ $x [$xs,*]) => `([$x, $xs,*])
125-  | _ => throw ()
126-
127--- END DETAILS
128-
129--- Now these all mean exactly the same thing:
130-
131-def mylist1 : NatList := 1 :: (2 :: (3 :: []))
132-def mylist2 : NatList := 1 :: 2 :: 3 :: []
133-def mylist3 : NatList := [1, 2, 3]
134-
135--- Some useful list-manipulation functions...
136-
137--- ### Repeat
138-
139-def myRepeat (n count : Nat) : NatList :=
140-  match count with
141-  | 0 => []
142-  | count' + 1 => n :: myRepeat n count'
143-
144--- Some simple facts about repetition:
145-
146-theorem repeat_zero (n : Nat) : myRepeat n 0 = [] := rfl
147-
148-theorem repeat_succ (n count : Nat) : myRepeat n (count + 1) = n :: myRepeat n count := rfl
149-
150-def length (l : NatList) : Nat :=
151-  match l with
152-  | [] => 0
153-  | _ :: t => (length t) + 1
154-
155--- Some simple facts about list lengths:
156-
157-theorem length_nil : [].length = 0 := rfl
158-
159-theorem length_cons (n : Nat) (l : NatList) : (n :: l).length = l.length + 1 := rfl

162-

164-  match l₁ with
165-  | [] => l₂
166-  | h :: t => h :: append t l₂

181-
182-theorem cons_append (n : Nat) (l₁ l₂ : NatList) : (n :: l₁) ++ l₂ = n :: (l₁ ++ l₂) := rfl
183-

228-
229--- Define a `count` function for `NatList`s that counts the
230--- number of times an element `n` appears in the list.
231-
232-def count (n : Nat) (l : NatList) : Nat := sorry
233-
234--- Now, prove these lemmas which should hold about your
235--- definition.
236-
237-theorem count_nil (n : Nat) : count n [] = 0 := sorry
238-
239-theorem count_cons_def (n h : Nat) (t : NatList) :
240-    count n (h :: t) = bif n == h then (count n t) + 1 else count n t := sorry
241-
242-theorem count_cons_same (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (t : NatList) (h : (n₁ == n₂) = true) :
243-    count n₁ (n₂ :: t) = count n₁ t + 1 := by
244-  sorry
245-
246-theorem count_cons_diff (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (t : NatList) (h : (n₁ == n₂) = false) :
247-    count n₁ (n₂ :: t) = count n₁ t := by
248-  sorry
249-
250-example : count 1 [1] = 1 := by
251-  rw [count_cons_same _ _ _ rfl]
252-  rw [count_nil]
253-
254-example : count 2 [2, 2] = 2 := sorry

256-theorem test_count1 : count 1 [1, 1, 4] = 2 := sorry
257-
258-theorem test_count2 : count 5 [1, 1, 4] = 0 := sorry

378--- ## Reasoning About Lists
379-
380--- As with numbers, some proofs about list functions need only
381--- rewriting...
382-
383--- ...and some need case analysis.
384-
385-theorem tail_length_pred (l : NatList) :
386-    l.length.pred = l.tail.length := by
387-  cases l with
388-  | nil       => rw [tail_nil, length_nil]; rfl
389-  | cons n l' => rw [tail_cons, length_cons]; rfl
390-
391--- Usually, though, interesting theorems about lists require
392--- induction for their proofs. We'll see how to do this next.
393-
394--- ### Induction on Lists
395-
396--- Lean generates an induction principle for every `inductive`
397--- definition, including lists. We can use the `induction`
398--- tactic on lists to prove things like the associativity of
399--- list-append...
400-
401-theorem append_assoc (l₁ l₂ l₃ : NatList) :
402-    (l₁ ++ l₂) ++ l₃ = l₁ ++ (l₂ ++ l₃) := by
403-  induction l₁ with
404-  | nil =>
405-    rw [nil_append, nil_append]
406-  | cons n l₁' ih =>
407-    rw [cons_append, cons_append, cons_append, ih]
408-
409--- For comparison, here is an informal proof of the same
410--- theorem.
411-
412--- *Theorem*: For all lists `l₁`, `l₂`, and `l₃`,
413-
414---   (l₁ ++ l₂) ++ l₃ = l₁ ++ (l₂ ++ l₃).
415-
416--- *Proof*: By induction on `l₁`.
417-
418--- - First, suppose `l₁ = []`. We must show
419-
420---   ([] ++ l₂) ++ l₃ = [] ++ (l₂ ++ l₃),
421-
422--- which follows directly from the definition of `append`.
423-
424--- - Next, suppose `l₁ = n :: l₁'`, with
425-
426---   (l₁' ++ l₂) ++ l₃ = l₁' ++ (l₂ ++ l₃)
427-
428--- (the induction hypothesis). We must show
429-
430---   ((n :: l₁') ++ l₂) ++ l₃ = (n :: l₁') ++ (l₂ ++ l₃).
431-
432--- By the definition of `append`, this follows from
433-
434---   n :: ((l₁' ++ l₂) ++ l₃) = n :: (l₁' ++ (l₂ ++ l₃)),
435-
436--- which is immediate from the induction hypothesis. *Qed*.
437-
438--- #### Generalizing Statements
439-
440--- Sometimes statements need to be generalized to prove them by
441--- induction:
442-
443-sf_expect_failure
444-  theorem myRepeat_append_fail (c n : Nat) :
445-      myRepeat n c ++ myRepeat n c = myRepeat n (c + c) := by
446-    induction c with
447-    | zero => rw [repeat_zero, nil_append]
448-    | succ c' ih =>
449-      rw [repeat_succ]
450-      -- Now we seem to be stuck.
451-      -- The `ih` only works for `c' + c'`,
452-      -- but we need `c' + 1 + (c' + 1)`.
453-
454--- unsolved goals
455--- case succ
456--- n c' : Nat
457--- ih : myRepeat n c' ++ myRepeat n c' = myRepeat n (c' + c')
458--- ⊢ (n :: myRepeat n c') ++ (n :: myRepeat n c') = myRepeat n (c' + 1 + (c' + 1))
459-
460--- A generalization that gives a stronger inductive hypothesis:
461-
462-theorem myRepeat_append_general (c₁ c₂ n : Nat) :
463-    myRepeat n c₁ ++ myRepeat n c₂ = myRepeat n (c₁ + c₂) := by
464-  induction c₁ with
465-  | zero =>
466-    rw [repeat_zero, Nat.zero_add, nil_append]
467-  | succ c1' ih =>
468-    rw [Nat.succ_add, repeat_succ, repeat_succ, cons_append, ih]
469-
470--- Then, we can use this more general theorem to prove the
471--- original goal:
472-
473-theorem myRepeat_append (c n : Nat) :
474-    myRepeat n c ++ myRepeat n c = myRepeat n (c + c) := by
475-  exact myRepeat_append_general c c n
476-
477--- #### Reversing a List
478-
479--- A more interesting example of induction over lists:
480-
481-def reverse (l : NatList) : NatList :=
482-  match l with
483-  | [] => []
484-  | h :: t => t.reverse ++ [h]
485-
486-theorem reverse_nil : [].reverse = [] := by rfl
487-
488-theorem reverse_cons (h : Nat) (t : NatList) : (h :: t).reverse = t.reverse ++ [h] := by rfl
489-
490-example : [1, 2, 3].reverse = [3, 2, 1] := by rfl
491-
492-example : [].reverse = [] := by rfl
493-
494--- Let's try to prove
495--- `∀ l : NatList, length (reverse l) = length l`.
496-
497-sf_expect_failure
498-  example (l : NatList) :
499-      l.reverse.length = l.length := by
500-    induction l with
501-    | nil => rw [reverse_nil]
502-    | cons n l' ih =>
503-      rw [reverse_cons]
504-      -- Now we seem to be stuck: the goal involves `++`,
505-      -- but we don't have any useful equations
506-      -- in either the immediate context or in the global
507-      -- environment!
508-
509--- unsolved goals
510--- case cons
511--- n : Nat
512--- l' : NatList
513--- ih : l'.reverse.length = l'.length
514--- ⊢ (l'.reverse ++ [n]).length = (n :: l').length
515-
516-sf_expect_failure
517-  theorem length_append_succ (l : NatList) (n : Nat) :
518-      (l.reverse ++ [n]).length = l.reverse.length + 1 := by
519-    induction l with
520-    | nil =>
521-      rw [reverse_nil, nil_append, length_cons, length_nil]
522-    | cons m l' ih =>
523-      rw [reverse_cons]
524-      -- `ih` not applicable
525-
526--- unsolved goals
527--- case cons
528--- n m : Nat
529--- l' : NatList
530--- ih : (l'.reverse ++ [n]).length = l'.reverse.length + 1
531--- ⊢ (l'.reverse ++ [m] ++ [n]).length = (l'.reverse ++ [m]).length + 1
532-
533-theorem append_length_succ (l : NatList) (n : Nat) :
534-    (l ++ [n]).length = l.length + 1 := by
535-  induction l with
536-  | nil => rw [nil_append, length_cons]
537-  | cons m l' ih =>
538-    rw [cons_append, length_cons, ih, length_cons]
539-
540--- Now we can prove the main theorem.
541-
542-theorem length_reverse (l : NatList) :
543-    l.reverse.length = l.length := by
544-  induction l with
545-  | nil => rw [reverse_nil]
546-  | cons n l' ih =>
547-    rw [reverse_cons, append_length_succ, ih, length_cons]
548-
549-theorem length_append (l₁ l₂ : NatList) :
550-    (l₁ ++ l₂).length = l₁.length + l₂.length := by
551-  sorry
552-

554-
555--- To prove the following theorem, which tactics will we need
556--- besides `intro`, `dsimp`, `rw`, and `rfl`?
557-
558--- (A) none
559-
560--- (B) `cases`
561-

576-
577--- To prove the following theorem, which tactics will we need
578--- besides `intro`, `dsimp`, `rw`, and `rfl`?
579-
580--- (A) none
581-
582--- (B) `cases`
583-
584--- (C) `induction` on `n`

588--- (E) can't be done with the tactics we've seen.

590--- ### List Exercises, Part 1
591-
592--- ### List Exercises, Part 2
593-
594-open NatList
595-
596--- ## Options
597-
598--- Suppose we'd like a function to retrieve the `n`th element
599--- of a list. What to do if the list is too short?
600-
601-def nthBad (l : NatList) (n : Nat) : Nat :=
602-  match l with
603-  | [] => 42
604-  | a :: l' => match n with
605-    | 0 => a
606-    | n' + 1 => nthBad l' n'
607-
608--- The solution: return a `NatOption`.
609-
610-end NatList
611-
612-inductive NatOption : Type where
613-  | some (n : Nat)
614-  | none
615-
616-namespace NatList
617-
618-def nth? (l : NatList) (n : Nat) : NatOption :=
619-  match l with
620-  | [] => .none
621-  | a :: l' => match n with
622-    | 0 => .some a
623-    | n' + 1 => nth? l' n'
624-
625-example : nth? [4, 5, 6, 7] 0 = .some 4 := by rfl
626-example : nth? [4, 5, 6, 7] 3 = .some 7 := by rfl
627-example : nth? [4, 5, 6, 7] 9 = .none := by rfl
628-
629-def NatOption.elim (d : Nat) (o : NatOption) : Nat :=
630-  match o with
631-  | .some n => n
632-  | .none => d
633-
634-theorem NatOption.elim_none (d : Nat) : elim d .none = d := by rfl
635-
636-theorem NatOption.elim_some (d₁ d₂ : Nat) : elim d₁ (.some d₂) = d₂ := by rfl
637-
638-end NatList
639-
640--- ## Partial Maps
641-
642--- As a final illustration of how data structures can be
643--- defined in Lean, here is a simple *partial map* data type,
644--- analogous to the map or dictionary data structures found in
645--- most programming languages.
646-
647--- First, we define a new type `MyId` to serve as the "keys" of
648--- our partial maps.
649-
650-structure MyId where
651-  val : Nat
652-
653--- Internally, a `MyId` is just a number. Introducing a
654--- separate type by wrapping each `Nat` makes definitions more
655--- readable and gives us flexibility to change representations
656--- later if we want to.
657-
658--- We'll also need an equality test for `MyId`s:
659-
660-def MyId.beq (x₁ x₂ : MyId) : Bool :=
661-  x₁.val == x₂.val
662-
663--- ### Exercise (1 star): MyId.beq_refl ⭐
664-
665-theorem MyId.beq_refl (x : MyId) : MyId.beq x x = true := by
666-  sorry
667-
668--- Now we define the type of partial maps:
669-
670-inductive PartialMap : Type where
671-  | empty : PartialMap
672-  | record (i : MyId) (n : Nat) (m : PartialMap) : PartialMap
673-
674-namespace PartialMap
675-
676--- The `update` function overrides the entry for a given key in
677--- a partial map by shadowing it with a new one (or simply adds
678--- a new entry if the given key is not already present).
679-
680-def update (d : PartialMap) (x : MyId) (value : Nat) : PartialMap :=
681-  record x value d
682-
683--- We can define functions on `PartialMap`s by pattern
684--- matching.
685-
686-def find (x : MyId) (d : PartialMap) : NatOption :=
687-  match d with
688-  | empty => .none
689-  | record y n d' =>
690-    bif MyId.beq x y then .some n
691-    else find x d'
692-
693--- _Quiz:_
694-
695--- Is the following claim true or false?
696-
697-theorem quiz1 (d : PartialMap) (x : MyId) (n : Nat) :
698-    find x (update d x n) = .some n := by
699-  dsimp [update, find]
700-  rw [MyId.beq_refl]
701-  dsimp
702-
703--- (A) True (B) False (C) Not sure
704-
705--- _Quiz:_
706-
707--- Is the following claim true or false?
708-
709-theorem quiz2  (d : PartialMap) (x y : MyId) (o : Nat) :
710-    MyId.beq x y = false →
711-    find x (update d y o) = find x d := by
712-  intro h
713-  dsimp [update, find]
714-  rw [h]
715-  dsimp
716-
717--- (A) True (B) False (C) Not sure
718-
719-end PartialMap
720-
721-end Lists
722-

LF/Logic.lean

1-import LF.Basics
2-import LF.Induction
3-import LF.Poly
4-import LF.Tactics
5-import LF.CustomTactics
6-
7-import SFLCompat
8-
9--- # Logic in Lean
10-
11--- Note to developers (before next release):
12---     Unlike earlier chapters, there are probably too many
13---     WORKINCLASSes in this chapter. BCP 20: But conversely
14---     some more quizzes would be great!
15-
16--- So far, we have seen:
17-
18--- - *propositions*: mathematical statements, so far only of 3
19---   kinds:
20-
21---   - equality propositions (`e1 = e2`)
22---   - implications (`a -> b`)
23---   - quantified propositions (`∀ x, a`)
24-
25--- - *proofs*: ways of presenting evidence for the truth of a
26---   proposition
27-
28--- In this chapter we will introduce several more flavors of
29--- both propositions and proofs.
30-
31--- Like everything in Lean, well-formed propositions have a
32--- *type*:
33-
34--- ## The `Prop` Type
35-
36-#check (∀ n m : Nat, n + m = m + n : Prop)
37-
38--- Note that *all* syntactically well-formed propositions have
39--- type `Prop` in Lean, regardless of whether they are true or
40--- not.
41-
42--- Simply *being* a proposition is one thing; being *provable*
43--- is a different thing!
44-
45-#check (2 = 2 : Prop)
46-#check (3 = 2 : Prop)
47-#check (∀ n : Nat, n = 2 : Prop)
48-
49--- So far, we've seen one primary place where propositions can
50--- appear: in `theorem` declarations.
51-
52-theorem plus_2_2_is_4 : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl
53-
54--- Propositions are first-class entities. For example, we can
55--- name them:
56-
57-def PlusClaim : Prop := 2 + 2 = 4
58-
59-#check PlusClaim
60-
61--- PlusClaim : Prop
62-
63-theorem plusClaim_is_true : PlusClaim := rfl
64-
65--- We can also write *parameterized* propositions — that is,
66--- functions that take arguments of some type and return a
67--- proposition.
68-
69-def Nat.IsThree (n : Nat) : Prop := n = 3
70-
71-#check (Nat.IsThree)
72-
73--- Nat.IsThree : Nat → Prop
74-
75--- In Lean, functions that return propositions are said to
76--- define *properties* of their arguments.
77-
78--- For instance, here's a (polymorphic) property defining the
79--- familiar notion of an *injective function*.
80-
81-def Injective {α β : Type} (f : α → β) : Prop :=
82-  ∀ x y : α, f x = f y → x = y

85-  intro x y h

89--- that returns a `Prop`. The expression `n = m` is notation
90--- for `Eq n m`. Because `Eq` can be used with elements of any

183--- ## Logical Connectives
184-
185--- ### Conjunction
186-
187--- The *conjunction*, or *logical and*, of propositions `a` and
188--- `b` is written `a ∧ b`; it represents the claim that both
189--- `a` and `b` are true.
190-
191-example : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
192-  /- A proof of a conjunction is a pair of proofs of the two components.
193-      To prove a conjunction, we build a pair using `constructor`. -/
194-  constructor
195-  · rfl /- 3 + 4 = 7 -/
196-  · rfl /- 2 * 2 = 4 -/
197-
198--- The constructor for conjunction is `And.intro`, which
199--- concludes that `a ∧ b` given that `a` and `b` hold
200--- individually.
201-
202-#check And.intro
203-
204--- And.intro {a b : Prop} (left : a) (right : b) : a ∧ b
205-
206--- We can also apply the constructor for the conjunction
207--- explicitly.
208-
209-example : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
210-  apply And.intro
211-  · rfl /- 3 + 4 = 7 -/
212-  · rfl /- 2 * 2 = 4 -/
213-
214--- Rather than applying the constructor, we can explicitly
215--- provide the arguments to the constructor as an `exact`
216--- proof.
217-
218-example : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
219-  exact And.intro rfl rfl
220-
221--- We can also use Lean's anonymous constructor notation
222--- `⟨..., ...⟩`, which works on constructors for proofs as
223--- well.
224-
225-example : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
226-  exact ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
227-
228--- So much for proving conjunctive statements. To go in the
229--- other direction — i.e., to *use* a conjunctive hypothesis to
230--- help prove something else — we can use `obtain` to obtain
231--- the components.
232-
233-example (n m : Nat) : n = 0 ∧ m = 0 → n + m = 0 := by
234-  sorry
235-
236--- We can also match on `h` right at the point where we
237--- introduce it, instead of introducing and then destructing
238--- it:
239-
240-example (n m : Nat) : n = 0 ∧ m = 0 → n + m = 0 := by
241-  intro ⟨hn, hm⟩
242-  rw [hn, hm]
243-
244--- For the present example, both ways work. But in other
245--- situations, we may wind up with a conjunctive hypothesis in
246--- the middle of a proof...
247-
248-example (n m : Nat) (h : n + m = 0) : n * m = 0 := by
249-  sorry
250-
251--- The infix notation `∧` is actually just syntactic sugar for
252--- `And a b`. That is, `And` is a Lean operator that takes two
253--- propositions as arguments and yields a proposition.
254-
255-#check And
256-
257--- And (a b : Prop) : Prop
258-
259--- ### Disjunction
260-
261--- Another important connective is the *disjunction*, or
262--- *logical or*, of two propositions: `a ∨ b` is true when
263--- either `a` or `b` is. This infix notation stands for
264--- `Or a b`, where `Or : Prop -> Prop -> Prop`.
265-
266--- To use a disjunctive hypothesis in a proof, we proceed by
267--- case analysis — which, as with other data types like `Nat`,
268--- is done using `cases`. The two cases are `inl` (for "left
269--- injection", or "in the left case") and `inr` (for "right
270--- injection", or "in the right case").
271-
272-theorem Nat.factor_is_zero (n m : Nat) (h : n = 0 ∨ m = 0) : n * m = 0 := by
273-  cases h with
274-  /- `n = 0` -/
275-  | inl hn => rw [hn, Nat.zero_mul]
276-  /- `m = 0` -/
277-  | inr hm => rw [hm, Nat.mul_zero]
278-
279--- Rather than performing case analysis via `cases`, we can
280--- also use `obtain` to match on the two possible injections,
281--- much like with `obtain` and `∧`.
282-
283-theorem and_is_false (b1 b2 : Bool) (h : (b1 = false) ∨ (b2 = false)) :
284-    (b1 && b2) = false := by
285-  obtain hb1 | hb2 := h
286-  · rw [hb1, Bool.false_and]
287-  · rw [hb2, Bool.and_false]
288-
289--- Conversely, to show that a disjunction holds, it suffices to
290--- show that one of its sides holds. This can be done via the
291--- tactics `left` and `right`. As their names imply, the first
292--- one requires proving the left side of the disjunction, while
293--- the second requires proving the right side. Here is a
294--- trivial use...
295-
296-theorem or_intro_l (a b : Prop) (h : a) : a ∨ b := by
297-  left; exact h
298-
299--- ... and here is a slightly more interesting example
300--- requiring both `left` and `right`:
301-
302-theorem Nat.zero_or_succ (n : Nat) : n = 0 ∨ n = (n + 1).pred := by
303-  sorry
304-

306-
307-theorem Nat.mul_is_zero (n m : Nat) (h : n * m = 0) : n = 0 ∨ m = 0 := by
308-  sorry
309-

311-
312-theorem or_commute (a b : Prop) (h : a ∨ b) : b ∨ a := by
313-  sorry

315--- ### Falsehood and Negation
316-
317--- Up to this point, we have mostly been concerned with proving
318--- "positive" statements — addition is commutative, appending
319--- lists is associative, etc. We are sometimes also interested
320--- in negative results, demonstrating that some proposition is
321--- *not* true. Such statements are expressed with the logical
322--- negation operator `¬`, which is a prefix notation for `Not`.
323-
324--- To see how negation works, recall the *principle of
325--- explosion* from the `Tactics` chapter, which asserts that,
326--- if we assume a contradiction, then any other proposition can
327--- be derived.
328-
329--- Following this intuition, we could define `¬ a` ("not `a`")
330--- as `∀ c, a → c`. Lean makes an equivalent but slightly
331--- different choice, defining `¬ a` as `a → False`, where
332--- `False` is a specific unprovable proposition defined in the
333--- standard library.
334-
335-#check Not
336-#print Not
337-
338-example (a : Prop) : Not a = (a → False) := rfl
339-example (a : Prop) : (¬ a) = (a → False) := rfl
340-
341--- Not (a : Prop) : Prop
342-
343--- @[implicit_reducible] def Not : Prop → Prop :=
344--- fun a => a → False
345-
346--- Since `False` is a contradictory proposition, the principle
347--- of explosion also applies to it. If we can get `False` into
348--- the context, we can use `cases` on it to complete any goal:
349-
350-theorem ex_falso_quodlibet (a : Prop) (h : False) : a := by
351-  cases h
352-
353--- Inequality is a very common form of negated statement, so
354--- there is a special notation for it: `≠`, which is infix
355--- notation for `Ne`.
356-
357-#print Ne
358-
359--- @[reducible] def Ne.{u} : {α : Sort u} → α → α → Prop :=
360--- fun {α} a b => ¬a = b
361-
362-theorem zero_not_one : 0 ≠ 1 := by
363-  /- The proposition `0 ≠ 1` is exactly the same as `¬ (0 = 1)`
364-      — that is, `Not (0 = 1)` — which unfolds to `(0 = 1) → False`. -/
365-  /- To prove an inequality, we may assume the opposite equality... -/
366-  intro contra
367-  /- ...and deduce a contradiction from it. Here, the equality
368-      `0 = 1` corresponds to `zero = succ zero`, which contradicts
369-      disjointness of constructors `zero` and `succ`, so `contradiction`
370-      takes care of it. -/
371-  contradiction
372-
373--- It takes a little practice to get used to working with
374--- negation in Lean. Even though *you* may see perfectly well
375--- why a claim involving negation holds, it can be a little
376--- tricky at first to see how to make Lean understand it!
377-
378--- Here are proofs of a few familiar facts to help get you
379--- warmed up.
380-
381-theorem not_False : ¬ False := by
382-  intro h; exact h
383-
384-theorem contradiction_implies_anything (a b : Prop) (h : a ∧ ¬ a) : b := by
385-  sorry
386-
387-theorem double_neg (a : Prop) (ha : a) : ¬ ¬ a := by
388-  sorry
389-
390--- Since inequality involves a negation, getting comfortable
391--- with it also often requires a little practice.
392-
393--- A useful trick: if you are trying to prove a nonsensical
394--- goal, apply `ex_falso_quodlibet` to change the goal to
395--- `False`. This makes it easier to use assumptions of the form
396--- `¬ a`, and in particular of the form `x ≠ y`.
397-
398-theorem not_true_is_false (b : Bool) (h : b ≠ true) : b = false := by
399-  cases b with
400-  | false => rfl
401-  | true =>
402-    dsimp [Ne, Not] at h
403-    apply ex_falso_quodlibet
404-    apply h
405-    rfl

520--- ## Truth
521-
522--- Besides `False`, Lean's standard library also defines
523--- `True`, a proposition that is trivially true. To prove it,
524--- we use the constructor `True.intro` explicitly, or the
525--- anonymous constructor `⟨⟩`, or the `constructor` tactic.
526-
527-example : True := by exact True.intro
528-example : True := True.intro
529-example : True := by exact ⟨⟩
530-example : True := ⟨⟩
531-example : True := by constructor
532-
533--- Unlike `False`, which is used extensively, `True` is used
534--- relatively rarely: it is trivial (and therefore
535--- uninteresting) to prove as a goal, and it provides no useful
536--- information when it appears as a hypothesis.
537-
538--- ### Logical Equivalence
539-
540--- The handy "if and only if" connective, which asserts that
541--- two propositions have the same truth value, is a structure
542--- containing the two implication directions. `a ↔ b` is
543--- notation for `Iff a b`.
544-
545--- You can use `Iff.mp` to access the forward direction of the
546--- iff, `Iff.mpr` to access the backwards direction, and
547--- `Iff.intro` to convert a goal of the form `a ↔ b` to two
548--- goals of the form `a → b` and `b → a`.
549-
550-#check (fun α β : Prop => α ↔ β : Prop → Prop → Prop)
551-
552-#check Iff
553-#check Iff.intro
554-#check Iff.mp
555-#check Iff.mpr
556-
557--- Iff (a b : Prop) : Prop
558-
559--- Iff.intro {a b : Prop} (mp : a → b) (mpr : b → a) : a ↔ b
560-
561--- Iff.mp {a b : Prop} (self : a ↔ b) : a → b
562-
563--- Iff.mpr {a b : Prop} (self : a ↔ b) : b → a
564-
565-theorem iff_sym (a b : Prop) (h : a ↔ b) : b ↔ a := by
566-  sorry

568-theorem not_true_iff_false (b : Bool) : b ≠ true ↔ b = false := by
569-  constructor
570-  · apply not_true_is_false
571-  · intro h; rw [h]; intro h'; contradiction

624--- ## Recap: Logical Connectives in Lean
625-
626--- Connectives introduced in this chapter:
627-
628--- - `a ∧ b` (conjunction):
629-
630---   - introduced with `constructor`
631---   - eliminated with `intro ⟨ha, hb⟩` or `obtain ⟨ha, hb⟩ := h`
632-
633--- - `a ∨ b` (disjunction):
634-
635---   - introduced with `left` and `right`
636---   - eliminated with `cases` or `obtain h | h := h`
637-
638--- - `False` (falsehood):
639-
640---   - eliminated with `cases` or `contradiction`
641-
642--- - `¬ a` (negation):
643-
644---   - defined as `a → False`
645-
646--- - `True` (truthhood):
647-
648---   - introduced as `True.intro` or with `constructor`
649-
650--- - `a ↔ b` (iff):
651-
652---   - introduced with `constructor`
653-
654---   - eliminated with `intro ⟨hab, hba⟩`,
655---     `obtain ⟨hab, hba⟩ := h`, or `Iff.mp` and `Iff.mpr`
656-
657--- - `∃ x : α, a` (existential):
658-
659---   - introduced with `exists y`
660---   - eliminated with `intro ⟨x, Hx⟩` or `obtain ⟨x, Hx⟩ := H`
661-
662--- Fundamental connectives we've been using since the
663--- beginning:
664-
665--- - equality (`x = y`)
666--- - implication (`a → b`)
667--- - universal quantification (`∀ x, a`)
668-
669--- ## Programming with Propositions
670-
671--- What does it mean to say that "an element `x` occurs in a
672--- list `l`"?
673-
674--- - If `l` is the empty list, then `x` cannot occur in it, so
675---   the property "`x` appears in `l`" is simply false.
676-
677--- - Otherwise, `l` has the form `[x' :: l']`. In this case, `x`
678---   occurs in `l` if it is equal to `x'` or if it occurs in
679---   `l'`.
680-
681--- We can translate this directly into a straightforward
682--- recursive function taking an element and a list and
683--- returning... a proposition!
684-
685-def List.In {α : Type} (x : α) (xs : List α) : Prop :=
686-  match xs with
687-  | [] => False
688-  | x' :: xs' => x = x' ∨ In x xs'
689-
690-theorem List.In_nil {α : Type} {x : α} : ¬ (List.In x []) := by
691-  dsimp [List.In]; intro h; assumption
692-
693-theorem List.In_cons {α : Type} {x x' : α} {xs : List α} : List.In x (x' :: xs) = (x = x' ∨ List.In x xs) := rfl
694-
695--- When `List.In` is applied to a concrete list, it expands
696--- into a concrete sequence of nested disjunctions.
697-
698-example : List.In 4 [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] := by
699-  sorry
700-
701-example (n : Nat) (h : List.In n [2, 4]) : ∃ n' : Nat, n = 2 * n' := by
702-  sorry
703-    /- (Notice the use of the empty pattern to discharge the last case.) -/
704-
705--- We can also reason about more generic statements involving
706--- `List.In`.
707-
708-theorem List.In_map {α β : Type} {f : α → β} {xs : List α} {x : α} (h : In x xs) :
709-    In (f x) (map f xs) := by
710-  induction xs with
711-  | nil =>
712-    exfalso; apply In_nil; assumption
713-  | cons x' xs' ih =>
714-    rw [In_cons] at h
715-    obtain h | h := h
716-    · rw [h, map_cons, In_cons]; left; rfl
717-    · rw [map_cons, In_cons]; right; exact ih h
718-
719--- ## Applying Theorems to Arguments
720-
721--- Lean also treats *proofs* as first-class objects!
722-
723--- We have seen that we can use `#check` to ask Lean whether an
724--- expression has a given type:
725-
726-#check (Nat.add : Nat → Nat → Nat)
727-
728--- We can also use it to check what theorem a particular
729--- identifier refers to:
730-
731-#check Nat.add_comm
732-
733--- Nat.add_comm (n m : Nat) : n + m = m + n
734-
735-#check Nat.add_assoc
736-

739--- Lean checks the *statements* of the `Nat.add_comm` and
740--- `Nat.add_assoc` theorems in the same way that it checks the
741--- *type* of any term (e.g. `Nat.add`). Leaving off the colon
742--- and the type, Lean prints these types in the infoview for
743--- us.
744-
745--- Why?
746-
747--- The reason is that the identifier `Nat.add_comm` actually
748--- refers to a *proof object* — a logical derivation
749--- establishing the truth of the statement
750--- `∀ n m : Nat, n + m = m + n`. The type of this object is the
751--- proposition that it is a proof of.
752-
753--- The type of an ordinary function tells us what we can do
754--- with it.
755-
756--- - If we have a term of type `Nat → Nat → Nat`, we can give it
757---   two `Nat`s as arguments and get a `Nat` back. Similarly, the
758---   statement of a theorem tells us what we can use that theorem
759---   for.
760-
761--- - If we have a term of type
762---   `∀ n m : Nat, n = m → n + n = m + m`, and we provide it two
763---   numbers `n` and `m` and a third "argument" of type `n = m`,
764---   we get back a proof object of type `n + n = m + m`.
765-
766--- Lean actually allows us to *apply* a theorem as if it were a
767--- function. This is often handy in proof scripts — e.g.,
768--- suppose we want to prove the following:

910--- ## Working with Decidable Properties
911-
912--- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims
913--- in Lean: with *booleans* (of type `Bool`), and with
914--- *propositions* (of type `Prop`). Here are the key
915--- differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
916-
917---   |                     | `Bool` | `Prop` |
918---   | ------------------- | ------ | ------ |
919---   | decidable?          | yes    | no     |
920---   | useable with match? | yes    | no     |
921-
922--- Since functions in Lean by default must terminate on all
923--- inputs, a terminating function of type `Nat → Bool` is a
924--- *decision procedure* — i.e., it yields `true` or `false` on
925--- all inputs.
926-
927--- For example, `Nat.even` is a decision procedure for the
928--- property "is even".
929-
930--- Since `Prop` includes *both* decidable and undecidable
931--- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a
932--- property that happens to be decidable: we can express it
933--- either as a boolean computation, or as a function into
934--- `Prop`.
935-
936--- For instance, to claim that a number `n` is even, we can say
937--- either that `Nat.even n` evaluates to `true`...
938-
939-example : Nat.even 42 = true := rfl
940-
941--- ... or that there exists some `k` such that `n = double k`.
942-
943-example : Nat.Even 42 := by dsimp [Nat.Even]; exists 21
944-
945--- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two
946--- characterizations of evenness did not describe the same set
947--- of natural numbers! Fortunately, they do!
948-
949--- To prove this, we first need two helper lemmas.
950-
951-theorem even_double (k : Nat) :
952-    Nat.even (Nat.double k) = true := by
953-  induction k with
954-  | zero => rw [Nat.double_zero]; rfl
955-  | succ k' ih => rw [Nat.double_succ]; exact ih
956-
957--- Note to developers (Yipeng Liu @berberman):
958---     Same issue as `CombineOddEven`.
959-
960-theorem even_double_conv (n : Nat) : ∃ k : Nat,
961-    n = bif Nat.even n then Nat.double k else Nat.double k + 1 := by
962-  sorry
963-
964--- Now the main theorem:
965-
966-theorem Nat.even_bool_prop (n : Nat) : Nat.even n = true ↔ Even n := by
967-  constructor
968-  · intro h
969-    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := even_double_conv n
970-    rw [h] at hk; dsimp at hk; dsimp [Even]; exists k
971-  · intro ⟨k, hk⟩; rw [hk]; apply even_double
972-
973--- In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean
974--- computation `Nat.even n` is *reflected* in the truth of the
975--- proposition `∃ k, n = Nat.double k`.
976-
977--- Similarly, to state that two numbers `n` and `m` are equal,
978--- we can say either
979-
980--- 1. that `n == m` returns `true`, or
981--- 2. that `n = m`.
982-
983--- Again, these two notions are equivalent:
984-
985--- (For the reverse direction we need the simple fact that `==`
986--- is reflexive.)
987-
988--- Note to developers (Yipeng Liu @berberman):
989---     Either get rid of the development of `beq` story or use
990---     our own `beq` on `Nat`.
991-
992--- Don't worry too much about `Nat.beq_eq_true_eq` yet, we need
993--- this from Lean because `n == m` is a wrapper of
994--- `DecidableEq Nat`. We will go over this in the Typeclasses
995--- chapter.
996-
997-theorem beq_eq_true (n m : Nat) :
998-    (n == m) = true ↔ n = m := by
999-  rw [Nat.beq_eq_true_eq]
1000-
1001--- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be
1002--- formalized as either a proposition or a boolean computation?
1003--- Which should we choose?
1004-
1005--- In general, *both* can be useful. For example, booleans are
1006--- more useful for defining functions, since we can test
1007--- whether they are true using conditional expressions.
1008-
1009-def is_even_prime (n : Nat) : Bool :=
1010-  bif n == 2 then true else false
1011-
1012--- The most direct way to prove this is to give the value of
1013--- `k` explicitly.
1014-
1015-example : Nat.Even 100 := by
1016-  exists 50
1017-
1018--- The proof of the corresponding boolean statement is simpler,
1019--- because we don't have to invent the witness `50`:
1020--- computation does it for us!
1021-
1022-example : Nat.even 100 = true := rfl
1023-
1024--- Now, the useful observation is that, since the two notions
1025--- are equivalent, we can use the boolean formulation to prove
1026--- the other one without mentioning the value 50 explicitly:
1027-
1028-example : Nat.Even 100 := by
1029-  obtain ⟨h, _⟩ := Nat.even_bool_prop 100
1030-  apply h; rfl
1031-
1032--- Although we haven't gained much in terms of proof-script
1033--- simplicity in this case, larger proofs can often be made
1034--- considerably simpler by the use of reflection.
1035-
1036--- As an extreme example, a famous mechanized proof of the even
1037--- more famous *four colour theorem* uses reflection to reduce
1038--- the analysis of hundreds of different cases to a boolean
1039--- computation.
1040-
1041--- Another advantage of booleans is that the *negation* of a
1042--- claim about booleans is straightforward to state and (when
1043--- true) to prove: simply flip the expected boolean result.
1044-
1045-example : Nat.even 101 = false := rfl
1046-
1047--- In contrast, propositional negation can be difficult to work
1048--- with directly. For example, suppose we state the nonevenness
1049--- of `101` propositionally:
1050-
1051--- Proving this directly — by assuming that there is some `n`
1052--- such that `101 = Nat.double n` and then somehow reasoning to
1053--- a contradiction — would be rather complicated.
1054-
1055--- But if we convert it to a claim about the boolean `Nat.even`
1056--- function, we can let Lean do the work for us.
1057-
1058-example : ¬ Nat.Even 101 := by
1059-  sorry
1060-
1061--- Conversely, there are situations where it can be easier to
1062--- work with propositions rather than booleans. In particular,
1063--- knowing that `(n == m) = true` is generally of little direct
1064--- help in the middle of a proof involving `n` and `m`. But if
1065--- we convert the statement to the equivalent form `n = m`,
1066--- then we can easily rewrite with it.
1067-
1068-theorem add_beq_true (n m p : Nat) (h : (n == m) = true) :
1069-    (n + p == m + p) = true := by
1070-  sorry

1072--- ## The Logic of Lean
1073-
1074--- Lean's logical core is a "metalanguage for mathematics" in
1075--- the same sense as familiar foundations for paper-and-pencil
1076--- math, like Zermelo–Fraenkel Set Theory (ZFC).
1077-
1078--- Mostly, the differences are not too important, but a few
1079--- points are useful to understand.
1080-
1081--- ### Propositional Extensionality
1082-
1083--- Lean's logic is quite minimalistic. This means that one
1084--- occasionally encounters cases where translating standard
1085--- mathematical reasoning into Lean is cumbersome - or even
1086--- impossible - unless we enrich its core logic with additional
1087--- axioms.
1088-
1089--- A first instance has to do with equality of propositions.
1090-
1091-#check (∀ a b : Prop, (a ∧ b) = (b ∧ a) : Prop)
1092-
1093--- This is an equality between two conjunctions, which itself
1094--- is also a proposition. It states that commuted conjunctions
1095--- are equal propositions. However, we cannot prove this
1096--- equality by reflexivity, as the two sides don't compute to
1097--- the same term, and we cannot proceed by cases on `a` or `b`,
1098--- as they are not inductive.
1099-
1100-sf_expect_failure
1101-  example (a b : Prop) : a ∧ b = b ∧ a := by rfl
1102-
1103--- Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side
1104---   a
1105--- is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
1106---   b = b ∧ a

1144--- we have seen earlier.

1148--- and_comm {a b : Prop} : a ∧ b ↔ b ∧ a
1149-
1150--- Since it would be convenient to be able to rewrite
1151--- propositions from one side of `↔` to the other, Lean
1152--- provides an axiom to turn `↔` into `=`, which is called
1153--- *propositional extensionality* (`propext`).
1154-
1155-#print propext
1156-
1157--- axiom propext : ∀ {a b : Prop}, (a ↔ b) → a = b
1158-
1159--- Lean provides an `ext` tactic that applies `propext` for us.
1160--- We can use it to show that commuted conjoined propositions
1161--- are equal. Similarly, we can use it to show that
1162--- reassociated conjoined propositions are equal as well.
1163-
1164-theorem and_comm_eq (a b : Prop) : (a ∧ b) = (b ∧ a) := by
1165-  ext; apply and_comm
1166-
1167-theorem and_assoc_eq (a b c : Prop) : ((a ∧ b) ∧ c) = (a ∧ (b ∧ c)) := by
1168-  ext; apply and_assoc
1169-
1170--- Here is an example of where using `=` instead of `↔` is more
1171--- convenient: we show that it's possible to "flip" three
1172--- conjoined propositions.
1173-
1174--- One way to prove this is to construct the `↔`, destruct the
1175--- `↔`s provided by `and_comm` and `and_assoc`, and apply the
1176--- resulting implications a few times. But this is a lot of
1177--- hassle, when the proof is conceptually simple: we flip `b`
1178--- and `c`, then we flip that conjunction with `a`, and we
1179--- finish by associativity. By using `and_comm_eq`, this is
1180--- easily done by rewriting equal propositions.
1181-
1182-theorem and_comm_flip (a b c : Prop) : (a ∧ b ∧ c) ↔ (c ∧ b ∧ a) := by
1183-  rw [and_comm_eq b c, and_comm_eq a, and_assoc_eq]
1184-
1185--- The pattern of deriving an equality of propositions out of
1186--- `↔` then rewriting by that equality is so common that Lean
1187--- will implicitly cast `↔` to `=`, allowing you to rewrite on
1188--- `↔` directly. Notice that `rw` is also able to close goals
1189--- of the form `a ↔ a` by reflexivity.
1190-

1192-  rw [@and_comm b c, @and_comm a, and_assoc]

1228--- ### Functional Extensionality
1229-
1230--- We can also write propositions claiming that two *functions*
1231--- are equal to each other. In some cases, we can also prove
1232--- that two functions are equal by reflexivity when both reduce
1233--- to the same expression:
1234-
1235-example : (fun x => x + 2) = (fun x => x + (Nat.pred 3)) := rfl
1236-
1237--- In general, functions can be equal for more interesting
1238--- reasons. In common mathematical practice, two functions `f`
1239--- and `g` are considered equal if they produce the same output
1240--- on every input:
1241-
1242---   (∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g
1243-
1244--- This is known as *functional extensionality*, which Lean
1245--- provides as `funext`.
1246-
1247-#check (fun f g => funext (f := f) (g := g) :
1248-    ∀ {α β : Type} (f g : α → β), (∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g)
1249-
1250--- Now we can prove some intuitively obvious equalities about
1251--- functions that would otherwise not be provable without
1252--- `funext`.
1253-
1254-theorem add_comm_fun : (fun (n m : Nat) => n + m) = (fun (n m : Nat) => m + n) := by
1255-  apply funext; intro n
1256-  apply funext; intro m
1257-  exact Nat.add_comm n m
1258-
1259--- The `ext` tactic will also apply `funext` as many times as
1260--- possible, introducing all variables in one go. (The singular
1261--- version of the tactic is `ext1`.)
1262-
1263-theorem add_comm_fun' : (fun (n m : Nat) => n + m) = (fun (n m : Nat) => m + n) := by
1264-  ext n m; exact Nat.add_comm n m

1272-

1276--- ### Classical vs. Constructive Logic
1277-
1278--- The following reasoning principle is *not* derivable with
1279--- the tools we've seen so far:
1280-
1281-def ExcludedMiddle := ∀ a : Prop, a ∨ ¬ a
1282-
1283--- Logical systems in which excluded middle does not hold are
1284--- referred to as *constructive logics*. They are so called
1285--- because to prove a proposition, we must give a construction
1286--- for it; for instance, a proof of `∃ x, p x` is proven by
1287--- providing a particular value of `x`.
1288-
1289--- Logical systems in which excluded middle does hold, such as
1290--- ZFC set theory, are referred to as *classical*. Lean
1291--- provides classical reasoning principles in the `Classical`
1292--- library, including excluded middle.
1293-
1294-#check Classical.em
1295-
1296--- Classical.em (p : Prop) : p ∨ ¬p

6--- # Poly: Polymorphism and Higher-Order Functions
7-
8--- ## Polymorphism
9-
10--- ### Polymorphic Lists
11-
12--- Instead of defining new lists for each type, like this...
13-
14-inductive BoolList : Type where
15-  | nil
16-  | cons (b : Bool) (l : BoolList)
17-
18--- ... Lean lets us give a *polymorphic* definition that allows
19--- list elements of any type:
20-
21-inductive MyList (α : Type) : Type where
22-  | nil : MyList α
23-  | cons (x : α) (l : MyList α) : MyList α
24-
25--- We can now write `MyList Nat` in place of a specialized
26--- list-of-numbers type.
27-
28--- What is `MyList` itself?
29-
30--- It is a *type constructor* — a function from types to types.
31-
32--- Note to developers (Yipeng Liu @berberman):
33---     A trick used below: parenthesizing the declaration makes
34---     it a term — Lean elaborates it and prints its inferred
35---     function type, instead of the declaration signature:
36---     `MyList (α : Type) : Type`.
37-
38-#check (MyList)
39-
40--- MyList : Type → Type
41-
42--- The `α` in the definition of `MyList` becomes an implicit
43--- parameter to the list constructors `nil` and `cons`.
44-
45-#check MyList.nil
46-
47--- MyList.nil {α : Type} : MyList α
48-
49-#check MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil
50-
51--- MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil : MyList Nat
52-
53-#check MyList.nil
54-
55--- MyList.nil {α : Type} : MyList α
56-
57-#check MyList.cons
58-
59--- MyList.cons {α : Type} (x : α) (l : MyList α) : MyList α
60-
61--- We can now define polymorphic versions of the functions
62--- we've already seen...
63-
64-def myRepeat (α : Type) (x : α) (count : Nat) : MyList α :=
65-  match count with
66-  | 0 => .nil
67-  | count' + 1 => .cons x (myRepeat α x count')
68-
69--- Some simple facts about `myRepeat`:
70-
71-theorem myRepeat_zero (α : Type) (v : α) :
72-    myRepeat α v 0 = MyList.nil := rfl
73-
74-theorem myRepeat_succ (α : Type) (v : α) (count : Nat) :
75-    myRepeat α v (count + 1) = MyList.cons v (myRepeat α v count) := rfl
76-
77-example : myRepeat Nat 4 2 = .cons 4 (.cons 4 .nil) := by rfl
78-
79-example : myRepeat Bool false 1 = .cons false .nil := by rfl
80-

82-
83--- What is the type of
84--- `MyList.cons true (MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil)`?
85-
86--- (A) `MyList Nat`
87-
88--- (B) `{α : Type} → α → MyList α → MyList α`
89-
90--- (C) `MyList Bool`
91-
92--- (D) `MyList (Nat × Bool)`
93-
94--- (E) Ill-typed
95-

97-
98--- What is the type of `myRepeat`?
99-
100--- (A) `Nat → Nat → MyList Nat`
101-
102--- (B) `(α : Type) → α → Nat → MyList α`
103-
104--- (C) `(α : Type) → {β : Type} → α → Nat → MyList β`
105-
106--- (D) Ill-typed
107-
108--- _Quiz:_
109-
110--- What is the type of `myRepeat 1 2`?
111-
112--- (A) `MyList Nat`
113-
114--- (B) `(α : Type) → α → Nat → MyList α`
115-
116--- (C) `MyList Bool`

118--- (D) Ill-typed

120--- From now on we'll use Lean's built-in `List α` type with
121--- notations `[]`, `::`, `[1, 2, 3]`, and `++`.
122-
123-example : List Nat := [1, 2, 3]
124-
125--- #### Type Annotation Inference
126-
127--- Let's write the definition of `myRepeat` again, but this
128--- time we won't specify the type of the parameter `α`. Will
129--- Lean still accept it?
130-
131-def myRepeat' α (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
132-  match count with
133-  | 0 => .nil
134-  | count' + 1 => .cons x (myRepeat' α x count')
135-
136--- Indeed it will. Lean infers that `α` is a type.
137-
138-#check myRepeat'
139-
140--- myRepeat'.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α
141-
142--- The generated `u_1` is part of Lean's bookkeeping for
143--- treating types more generally. We will not need to interpret
144--- names like this for now — you can ignore them when they
145--- appear in Lean's output unless we explicitly call attention
146--- to them.
147-
148--- Lean has used *type inference* to deduce a type for `α`.
149-
150--- #### Type Argument Synthesis
151-
152--- Supplying every type *argument* is also boring, but Lean can
153--- usually infer them:
154-
155-def myRepeat'' (α : Type) (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
156-  match count with
157-  | 0 => []
158-  | count' + 1 => x :: myRepeat'' _ x count'
159-
160--- Alternatively, we can declare arguments implicit by
161--- surrounding them with curly braces instead of parens:
162-
163-def myRepeat''' {α : Type} (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
164-  match count with
165-  | 0 => []
166-  | count' + 1 => x :: myRepeat''' x count'
167-
168--- #### Supplying Type Arguments Explicitly
169-
170--- In general, it's fine to just let Lean infer all type
171--- arguments. But occasionally this can lead to problems:
172-
173--- This fails because Lean can't figure out the type of the
174--- empty list: `def mynil := []` — error: type not known We can
175--- fix this with an explicit type annotation:
176-
177--- We can use the `@` prefix to supply the type argument
178--- explicitly. The `@` makes all implicit arguments of a
179--- function explicit:
180-
181-#check @List.nil
182-
183-def myNil' := @List.nil Nat
184-
185--- @List.nil : {α : Type u_1} → List α
186-

191--- list brackets.)
192-
193---   [1, 2, 3]

195--- (A) `List Nat`
196-

288-
289-def List.rev {α : Type} (l : List α) : List α :=
290-  match l with
291-  | .nil => .nil
292-  | .cons h t => rev t ++ (.cons h .nil)
293-
294-theorem rev_nil {α : Type} : ([] : List α).rev = [] := by rfl
295-
296-theorem rev_cons {α : Type} {x : α} {l : List α} :
297-    (x :: l).rev = l.rev ++ [x] := by rfl

299--- ### Exercise (2 stars): poly_exercises ⭐⭐
300-
301--- Here are a few simple exercises, just like ones in the Lists
302--- chapter, for practice with polymorphism. Complete the proofs
303--- below. You will likely find useful the following
304--- characterizing lemmas for `List.append` in Lean standard
305--- library:
306-
307-#check List.nil_append
308-#check List.cons_append
309-
310--- List.cons_append.{u} {α : Type u} {a : α} {as bs : List α} : a :: as ++ bs = a :: (as ++ bs)
311-
312--- List.nil_append.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : [] ++ as = as
313-
314-theorem append_nil {α : Type} {l : List α} :
315-    l ++ [] = l := by
316-  sorry
317-
318-theorem append_assoc {α : Type} {l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α} :
319-    l₁ ++ l₂ ++ l₃ = l₁ ++ (l₂ ++ l₃) := by
320-  sorry
321-
322-theorem append_length {α : Type} {l₁ l₂ : List α} :
323-    (l₁ ++ l₂).length = l₁.length + l₂.length := by
324-  sorry
325-
326--- ### Exercise (2 stars): more_poly_exercises ⭐⭐
327-
328--- Here are some slightly more interesting ones...
329-
330-theorem reverse_append {α : Type} {l₁ l₂ : List α} :
331-    (l₁ ++ l₂).rev = l₂.rev ++ l₁.rev := by
332-  sorry
333-
334-theorem reverse_reverse {α : Type} (l : List α) :
335-    l.rev.rev = l := by
336-  sorry
